utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alilovic. Mr. Alilovic, I would like us to go back to what you said at the end of your testimony yesterday. You said something that seemed a little puzzling to me, a bit unusual. I asked about what the boy you received in your house might have said. I asked you whether he had told you about everything that had happened. Do you remember what you said about this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember quite a lot because the young boy spent almost 13 days, 12 days with me, and we talked about quite a lot of things. I can say one thing: His father was not to blame for the last conflict, as much as he was to blame for the first one, but I said that he got it on his back. He even brought explosives from the Vitez company, the company in Vitez which was called Princip. He told me quite a lot of things. I have forgotten some of them after all these years, but I remember quite a lot. I don't know what else I could say about this young boy who stayed with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This young man told you that his brother had been killed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This young man also told you that they had tried to kill him?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He told me this: That his brother had been killed, that his brother had been killed some 20 metres away from their house, and that the other soldier had said, "The child is not to blame for anything. Let the child go." Another soldier told the young boy to go in the direction of the road, and that's what the boy did, where he was found by other soldiers who brought him to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us talk about those two soldiers, Mr. Alilovic, who brought the child to your home; did you know them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't know that I ever saw them again after that, but let me add that what I find interesting is that the soldier called me by my name, and yet I didn't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that. Did you see a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. A vehicle was parked in my yard or, rather, between the road and the yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type was the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us talk now about the three soldiers who arrived at your house after that. Two of them used the telephone. Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the soldiers or some of the soldiers who were in the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember that I knew any of them. There were a few soldiers in the Bungalow, but they had all come from elsewhere, and I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the Bungalow before that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since I have a meadow across from the Bungalow on the other side of the road, and I went to work in my meadow occasionally, I would come up to the Bungalow. There was no need to go into the Bungalow, and maybe I was forbidden to enter, but I never even tried to enter the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you know any of the soldiers who were there?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When those three soldiers came to your home, was Pezer's house already burning?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. It was set on fire early in the morning. The soldiers arrived at nine, and it was already burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see from which direction the soldiers had come, from Ahmici or from the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I was just awakened by gunfire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know in what direction they left? Did they leave in the direction of the Bungalow or Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The soldiers, who used the telephone at my house, left in the direction of the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now talk about the fourth soldier. If I understood you well, the fourth soldier arrived while the first three were still at your house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers, if I understood you well, had the same kind of uniform and the same insignia?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: One was wearing a black uniform, two were wearing camouflage uniforms, and the fourth soldier who arrived after them was also wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen the fourth soldier before?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it seems that there was some kind of connection with your wife's family?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No connection with him and my wife because my wife was from his village. She knew his mother and she knew his father, but she didn't know him because he belonged to the younger generation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To clarify this for the record, one of your answers is not in the record. You didn't know either the first three soldiers or the fourth soldier, and you had never seen any of these soldiers before?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that the fourth soldier was crying and that he mentioned the massacre of his family which had taken place in Dusina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, for the record, there was no response.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear any response by the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make everything quite clear for the record, I said, you didn't know any of the soldiers who came to your house in the morning, either the first three soldiers or the fourth soldier, and you had never seen them previously?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had never seen them before, and I didn't know them. I didn't know the younger soldier who came fourth. I didn't know him either. I didn't even know he was Jure Kegelj's son until he told us so himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know in what period the massacre of this soldier's family had taken place?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Three weeks after the -- before the second attack on Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will repeat the question again because I'm not sure you understood it properly. The young man was weeping because his family had been massacred in Dusina. You told us that yesterday. My question is the following: Do you know or did he tell you when this massacre had taken place?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I said, three weeks before that, the massacre had taken place, and the young soldier who came fourth hadn't been at home that day. His brothers and sister and mother and his brother's children were at home, so he went and left my house crying because he told me and my wife that they had killed his father, his mother, and five brothers, and that they had taken one of his brothers children, a four-year-old boy, and that they had impaled him. That's what he told me. There was nothing I could say to that. I just kept silent. I had no words to say to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what this man told you happened, as far as you know, three weeks before he told you about it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, three weeks before, he told me about it, three weeks before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this soldier had come from when he arrived at your house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know in which direction he left?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He left in the direction of the Bungalow with the other three soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they left together in the direction of the Bungalow, the three soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the four of them left together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday, Mr. Alilovic, that your brother Tomislav was very frightened by the presence of the soldiers. You also told us that he was afraid that the soldiers would somehow take him to the war with them.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My brother was in the next room, in another room, not the one where my wife and I were, when the three soldiers came in. There's a sliding door, so my brother kept the door slightly ajar. They saw him in the room, and they became frightened and said to him, "Why are you hiding?" But he wasn't hiding. That's how it turned out. They thought he was hiding, so they even pointed their weapons at him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why was he hiding from these soldiers? What was he afraid of; can you explain?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he wasn't hiding. He had just got out of bed, and he wasn't dressed yet, so he kept the door slightly ajar while he was getting dressed. It appeared as if he was hiding. The soldiers suspected that he was hiding because the door was not fully open but only slightly ajar. Then I said to them or, rather, they said to me, "Who is that there?" And I said, "It's my brother."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let me remind you, Mr. Alilovic, that yesterday you told us that your brother was very afraid of being mobilised.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Yes, my brother was quite afraid of being mobilised. That's why, within seven to ten days, he left again to Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how did he know that he was in danger of being mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the war broke out, and he is an able-bodied man, fit for military service, and whoever was fit for military service was called up. They had everyone come and fight with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell him that he was in danger?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. He could see for himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Tomislav older than you or younger?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear how many years.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- younger than me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday, Mr. Alilovic, that you were in excellent relations with Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic who were your neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I was on very good terms with all my neighbours, always. I never hated either the Muslims or the Croats or the Serbs, and I still don't hate any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You considered them your neighbours. Did they ever come to your home? Did you ever receive their visits?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. They would come for coffee at my house, and they would work on my meadows sometimes. We would go to help each other. We helped one another without drawing any distinctions. It didn't matter whether they were Muslims or Croats because that was the custom with everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember at that time that you would go to help others? I'm talking about April '93. Do you remember going to their house, either to Zoran Kupreskic's or Mirjan Kupreskic's house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you just said that you went there often.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, two or three years before that, but in 1993, I never went to see their parents at their house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993 or 1992, did Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic come to your house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they didn't. I don't remember that they did, and my wife didn't tell me that they had come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you said before that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic and yourself, that you met each other often, what time were you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking about Sundays, at some festivities, some meetings, assemblies, or some celebrations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said a while ago that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic could have worked in your fields, I think you said that, what time were you thinking then?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I said that Muslims could work in my fields, as they did, just like Kasim Pezer for years and years worked with my horses in the fields, and neither of the Kupreskics worked in my meadows. I don't remember that happening any year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order for everything to be quite clear, Mr. Alilovic, with the permission of the Court, I will ask one question: You said that at no time in that time -- and I'm talking about 1992 and 1993, so in that period, in no time did Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic come to your house nor to your property?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I said that they did not. There was no need for them to come, and they didn't come, and I didn't go to their house either. I don't remember going there, to either one of their houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, were you already in good relations, in excellent relations, like you said?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was in good relations with them always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I will be brief. Re-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor yesterday tried to make you out to be an unreliable witness by asking if there was any other Jozo Alilovic besides yourself, and that there had been some witnesses who had claimed that this Jozo Alilovic was at Radak's Bridge. Well, now I would like to know if there is another Jozo Alilovic or not. You said later that there is one such person in Vitez; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There is a Jozo Alilovic in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, his nickname is Bego.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he is different from you; he has this other nickname. Do you know any people from Donja Rovna?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the nickname "Josko" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I wanted to tell you. This is not the municipality of Vitez. He is in the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was asking, what was Josko's name?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: His name is Josko Alilovic. Maybe they write it as "Jozo," but we all call him "Josko."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you mention him yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I didn't mention him because he is not in the municipality of Vitez. He is in the municipality of Busovaca, so I didn't concentrate on Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This boy who was brought to you with the car and two soldiers, who was brought to your house, and we talked about him, but we will not mention his name: Did he know what your name was?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. Yes, he did know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it strange then, for these soldiers who were there to have known your name?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I said yesterday that it was strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That I didn't know any of those soldiers, but they knew me. He called me by my name, Jozo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So didn't that boy, when he stopped the car, perhaps, could have told them whose house that was?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he probably was the one who told them what my name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, in what period were you a gamekeeper, from what year to what year? Well, you said when you stopped going, but when did you start?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've been a gamekeeper for almost 20 years. I still am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the area where you were a gamekeeper?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was a hunter from the road which leads to Zenica, Poculica, Vjetrenica, up to Busovaca, Kaonik, and Kuber, all the way up there. That was my territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your brother, when the soldiers came, that he was in the next room, and that the door was ajar.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That room next door, was that in your old house or in the new house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the old house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that moment, this boy that we are talking about when the soldiers came to your house and when your brother was in the next room, where was the boy?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was in the kitchen, together with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which room did you talk to those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the kitchen. We were all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions. Mr. Alilovic, the Court is most grateful to you for coming to The Hague to testify. You may now be released. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, everyone. (The witness withdrew) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic. Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic. Would you please introduce yourself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Vidovic. I was born on the 10th of January, 1960, in the village of Pirici, municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Mr. Vidovic, point out on the aerial photograph next to you, indicate to us where your house is, where you lived at that time, and where you live today.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I stand up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please stand up.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is your house? Which part of the village is it in, and would you please indicate it to us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's 250 to 300 metres away from the main road, so that's somewhere in this area here (indicating). Right here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you find it on the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My house? Yes. It's here (indicating). It's right here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who your closest neighbours were, Croats, in that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My closest neighbours were the Kupreskics in the upper part, Mirko Vidovic, Gordana Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point those houses out on the aerial photograph in relation to your house.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Kupreskic homes are right here. The house of Gordana Vidovic is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mirko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mirko Vidovic is here as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were your closest Muslim neighbours in that part?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The closest Muslim neighbours were Suljo Pezer; his brother, Smajl Pezer --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what side of the road were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were on the right side of the road. Hazim Ahmic, Abdulah Ahmic, Sakib Pezer, and his son, Zakir Pezer. They're on the left side. So Sakib and Zakir Pezer were on the right side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The road that comes into Ahmici that branches off from the main road, could you show us in relation to that road how the houses were located, on what side were the Muslim houses, and where were the Croats in that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the Croats -- the Croats were on the left side, and the Muslims were on the right side. Three Croat houses were, however, on the right side. That was the house of Vlatko Kupreskic, Zoran Kupreskic, and Anto Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic's father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any Croat house on the right side of the road? If we look at this road, this main road that goes to Ahmici and then the road that goes to Upper Ahmici, on that side of the road, were there any Croat houses on that side of the road, when you look at this road towards Upper Ahmici, Gornji Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, there are no Croat houses there. They are all Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Vidovic. You may sit down. On this aerial photograph, you will indicate your house, and then you will keep this photograph because we will make some other markings on it too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So would the usher please give the aerial photograph to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D105/2.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My house?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, mark your house.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's this house on this side. What is this? Is that a kind of a wood next to your house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's a pine tree. It's a tree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also indicate on the aerial photograph where the house of Mirko Vidovic is in relation to your house? You don't need to mark it. You can just point it out. Just tell us which house it is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's right here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the house of Gordana Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this part, these were those three Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when the guards started in Ahmici? Who started the watches? Were they joint watches? How was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning the Muslims started the night watch first. This was perhaps in January or February of '92. Then in April or May, we Croats who were bordering the road also started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about the guards only in this part of the village, where you lived, or are you talking about guards in that entire region of Ahmici, Pirici, and Santici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am saying -- I'm only talking about the watches in that part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you started the night watches in April or May of '92. Do you have any other connections with the Muslim guards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the evening we would usually be together with them. We would go together along the road. Sometimes we would go this way, they would go up to their village, and then sometimes we would meet. We were together mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a kind of organised command --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- within the guard duty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Muslims have weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I could see when we would meet on that night watch, I only saw one rifle, which was carried by Omer Ahmic, and I think it was a handmade weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the Muslims arm themselves? Do you know when they received weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of May, I was at home, and then from the direction of Vitez, so from the main road going into Gornji Ahmici, a truck passed by my house, which was driven by Muhamed Pezer. That truck, I remember well, was green, and I saw in the truck a lot of weaponry, a lot of ammunition cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what kind of weapons they brought to the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the truck, I could see three Muslims who were standing there. One of them was standing there, and he was holding an M-53 machine gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what kind of weapons were there in the truck?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could see mostly that it was automatic -- that there were automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say this was the beginning of May in '92?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear or did you find out whether the Croats got weapons from Slimena?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that from anywhere, but I know that we Croats who were in that region did not receive anything. We didn't get anything from anybody, nor did we know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did these -- what you described as kind of joint guards, how long did they last?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, up until the summer, and then in the evening, on night watch, Mirko Vidovic and Mirjan Kupreskic were there, and they went inside the elementary school in Ahmici, but they were thrown out and they did not allow us Croats to enter that school any more. So from that time we didn't go on guard duty together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they have in the school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they had a radio transmitter, and they were on duty there all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What radio transmitter was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was a RUP 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that they kept the guard by the radio transmitter day and night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since I live nearby, only about 70 metres, approximately, away from the school, at night I would see a light on in that classroom, and I would see them pass by during the daytime, going to the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So after that you didn't have any more joint patrols?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say after all this whether it was an organised joint patrol, so that, for example, you would say, "Well, two Croats and two Muslims will go out every evening," or was it more like a walk taken together? Did you have some kind of schedule?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no schedule. We would happen to meet, and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in your part of the village -- and that is Pirici, where you said there were Croatian houses -- who kept watch? Who went on patrol? Which people from that part of the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the Croats?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the Croats.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will start with myself. Then there was Mirko Vidovic, Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Ivica Kupreskic. Then Mirko Sakic, Drago Grgic, Miro Samija, Nikola Samija. I don't know if I've enumerated them all. I can't remember any more, but there were about 14 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's how many you counted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, for example, Mirko Sakic. Did he go regularly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Sometimes we would quarrel about this, but he only went to patrol the village about two or three times, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider that it was his duty to patrol the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a villager, so I thought -- well, if it's my duty, it's his duty too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a member of the reserve police force for a time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the reserve police force in the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the reserve police was Zahid Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zahid Ahmic a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when weapons were handed out to the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It was sometime in 1991 when the reserve police was supplied with weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get a weapon then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have this weapon at your home? Did you keep it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, two or three months later, I received a notice from my company that I should report for work. So I went to work, and then I gave back my gun and my uniform from the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did you return the weapon and the uniform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since Zahid Ahmic was the commander, I gave it back to him. I gave the things back to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many reserve policemen were there in the village? Do you know who stayed on after you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was Zahid Ahmic and I think Kemo. I can't remember, but I think he stayed as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You only remember those two?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you say where you continued working?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Vjetrenica, the trading company where I had worked before, so I returned to the same job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had been sent home because there was not enough work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From March 1992 until when were you employed in Vjetrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I worked there until the start of the second conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Were you in an active HVO unit at any time before the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to a front line toward the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, because I was employed, so I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now talk about the first conflict that was in October 1992. What do you remember just before the outbreak of the conflict? What do you remember happened on the day before the 19th of October? Did you have any information that something was about to happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information. Everything appeared to be normal. I went to work as usual, came back from work as usual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that a roadblock was set up near the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that there was another checkpoint somewhere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew about the checkpoint on the road leading to Ahmici, at the entrance to Ahmici, because this checkpoint was there for a few days, and I would pass by when going to work in Vitez and coming back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on what road was this roadblock?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the very entrance into the village of Ahmici, some 15 or 20 metres away from the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did this roadblock look like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were two trestles, wooden trestles, and there was a beam across them. Down on the road, there were two anti-tank mines, one on each side of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything beside the road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was something. Something had been built out of blocks, so it was on the right-hand side when entering Ahmici, and they used this to sit down behind that wall. That's where they would sit when they were guarding the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this roadblock was there for a few days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the Muslims doing at this roadblock? What was their role?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They checked anyone entering the village. They would stop them and they would search them. In the evening, they would even stop me when I was coming back from Vitez, and when they saw it was me, they would let me pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they set up this roadblock on their own initiative or in agreement with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no agreement with the Croats. They set it up at their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Did you ask them what they were doing there? Did you tell them that your house was there? Did you complain when you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to them, but, of course, it wasn't that I didn't care about it because my home was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people at the roadblock, did they have uniforms or were they in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some of them had uniforms and some of them were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were armed. They had automatic weapons. Everyone who was at the checkpoint had an automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, on the 19th of October, what time did you usually come home from work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually I would come back from work at about half past three, 15.30, and it was the same that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people were at the roadblock then, and did you know them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many there were, but I think three, four, maybe five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they people you knew from the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was Suljo Ahmic; I remember him. Mines Ahmic and Suad Ahmic were there. I don't know who else. I can't remember any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do that day, that evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since I had come home from work, I did my daily chores. That evening, it was my turn to keep watch from 11.00 until 1.00 a.m., and I patrolled with Mirko Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these shifts organised? When did the patrols begin; when did they end? How long were the shifts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they started at 7.00 p.m. and ended at 7.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Your shift, you said it began at 11.00?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at 11.00 p.m. until 1.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything unusual happen that night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How can I say it? We were handing over our shift to the next two, and then we went to Niko Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Go on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then we were replaced by Miro Samija and Drago Grgic. Then Mirko Vidovic, who was keeping watch with me, went to his home, and I, of course, went to my home. As I was passing by Gordana Vidovic's cowshed, I saw, from the direction of Gornji or Upper Ahmici, a large group of armed soldiers coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since there is a good view from that cowshed in the direction of Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse where there was a light on, I could see very well. I could even have counted them, had I wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there approximately, in your estimate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately between 30 and 40 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed? Did you see whether they were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I concealed myself beside the cowshed and waited for them to pass by. They were about five metres away, and I saw that some of them were wearing uniforms and others were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see where they went?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, because I was interested, so I observed them, and this group entered the school, the primary school in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform anyone of this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I found this suspicious, such a big group coming at that time, but since they had had exercises before, I thought, "Well, maybe this is just something like that." So I didn't feel the need to inform anyone. I didn't think it was anything really special.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it usual at that time to see groups of armed men, 30 to 40 men, without reacting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, it wasn't usual. We'd never seen such a group before. But there had been no problems before, so I concluded that nothing would happen now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There had not been any conflicts before between the Croats and the Muslims; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. What did you do then after that? You saw these men; you saw them entering the school. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I went into my house and I went to bed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you wake up? What woke you up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at about 5.00 a.m., I was awakened by a powerful detonation. I got up. In fact, everyone who was in the house got up, my parents, my wife, my children. We were afraid. We got ready, and then we sat there, not knowing what was going on. After an hour and a half, at about half past six, we could hear intense gunfire coming from the direction of the mosque, the main road, and the cemetery, from that direction, because that was as far as I could tell from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave your house then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't leave the house. We couldn't get out because there were bullets flying around everywhere and even falling onto the roof of my house, so that we were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could hear the bullets falling?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, so we didn't dare leave the house. At around half past seven, approximately, there was a lull in the gunfire, and we fled to Niko Sakic's shelter, the shelter in the house of Niko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? Why did you go there? Why didn't you stay at home? Did your house have a basement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My house -- well, we were afraid of the gunfire. This was the first time we had experienced something like that. That was why we fled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you settled your family in Niko Sakic's basement, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't enter the shelter. I passed by the upper side of Niko's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you meet there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw my neighbours there, Slavko and Mirko Sakic, Zoran Kupreskic and Mirjan, his brother. There was Milutin Vidovic, Zdravko Vrebac, Miro Vidovic. There was Miroslav Pudza and some others. I may not remember all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was it approximately? Can you tell us whether it was in the morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was about a quarter to eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there in front of that house? Did you move away from there? Did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we didn't stay there long because bullets started flying up to that house too. We could hear twigs breaking in the trees, so we moved 20 or 30 metres away and went into a depression, which was a good natural shelter because the bullets couldn't hit us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the depression near Niko Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It's Ivo Kupreskic's property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please indicate on the aerial map what depression that is, whose area that is, whose forest? What is that forest called next to the depression?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's here (indicating) in this depression. The depression belongs to Ivo Kupreskic, and this forest here (indicating), it belongs to my father, Stipan Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that forest called?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Stipan's Forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were there in that depression?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were there, right here at the beginning of the depression (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. On that day, did you, in any way, participate in the events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, we stayed there the whole day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you sleep that night? Where did your family sleep?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That night I slept in the barn that belonged to Ivo Kupreskic, and my family was in the shelter in Niko Sakic's house. That's where they spent that one night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the barn of Ivo Kupreskic? Is that the house right next to the depression, in the section where the Kupreskic houses are?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the left side immediately when you leave the depression, it belongs to that family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the combat activities stop in the village? When did the gunfire stop? When did the situation calm down?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon, the gunfire stopped. It couldn't be heard anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice that Muslims were leaving the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime at around 11.00, from the depression, I went to my house to see what was going on there, to see if there was any damage. Then when I was coming back again towards the house of Niko Sakic, going towards the depression, I saw Muslims from Zume who were going in the direction of Gornji Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether your neighbours, your Muslim neighbours left the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They left the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they come back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe three or four days afterwards, they came back to their homes. You could see smoke from their chimneys which indicated that they were already back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who agreed on the terms of the return for the Muslims, and was this the way that the return was discussed, with some kind of conditions, preconditions, terms? Were there any kinds of talks with the Muslims like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember anything like that happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they return by themselves?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody guarantee their safety? Did they ask them to return their weapons? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that some were asking for the return of some four automatic rifles which were taken away at the roadblock by the Topole cemetery. I remember that that was one request, but I don't know about any other terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it agreed, in that time after the conflict, to try to set up a joint roadblock in Ahmici which would include Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that there was a meeting, and then at that meeting, there was a conclusion, an agreement, that was adopted to set up a checkpoint at the entrance to Ahmici and to have two Croats and two Muslims at that checkpoint, for them to control it together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this carried out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, yes. I remember well that I was also on duty once there. I was there with Zoran Kupreskic. So from us Croats, there was Zoran and myself, and then from the Muslims, there was Mines Ahmic and Suljo Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did that checkpoint last in that composition?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that didn't really last that long. I didn't serve more than one shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the Croats took care to protect the Muslim homes during the time that the Muslims were away? Did they organise watches around those houses?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Croats who were close to those Muslim houses naturally took care so that there would be no break-ins or no thefts because things like that did happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us about the 19th? This is the day before the conflict. Do you remember, did you see Zoran Kupreskic on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I came back from work, so at about 3.30 in the afternoon, I had a call from Zoran Kupreskic, and he asked me, could I go with him to bring back some boards. I helped him to do that. I had a truck, so we unloaded these boards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you bring those boards from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We got them from Rovna, and I helped him unload that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the first conflict, after the 20th of October, 1992, did you see armed Muslims in the village, in your part of the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I saw them passing, and they had weapons. I saw them during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they carry on with their guards, and did they carry out that guard duty with guns?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they carried on, and they performed that duty while armed. They carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them going to the front, the Muslims? Did they go to the front?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had a front close to Visoko at that time, at Cekrcici, to be precise, so I know that they went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see how they went to the front? Did they have equipment or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, they went to the front with weapons. Some had uniforms; some didn't. They would gather. Their collection point was in front of the Ahmici school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your house was close to that school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's less than 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would see them in front of the school; that was their collection point, departure point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big were those groups? How large were those shifts of people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I think perhaps there would be groups of 20 people approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice them when they would come back to the village from the front?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's why I remembered it so well. When they came back from the front, they would line up there again. Then for the first time, it was the first time that I had heard some of those orders and commands, "Tegbir," "Allah-u-ekber," and after that, they would fire rounds of gunfire. It wasn't something that was pleasant to hear so close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in the beginning that people, Croats, didn't have weapons when you started the guards. I'm not talking about all Croats now from the village, but I'm just talking about you and the members of your guard, the people who participated in the guard duty with you. When did they obtain weapons; can you say that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say for certain when I obtained weapons, so that was with the fall of Jajce. There were a lot of refugees from Jajce, so you could buy them from them. I bought a semi-automatic rifle for myself, a PAP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other people that you mentioned who were around the house of Niko Sakic on the 20th, were they all your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So some of them you saw in the guards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those people have weapons during the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Only one. I remember Mirko Sakic only had a hunting rifle. The rest of us didn't have weapons. I don't remember seeing any with anybody else, and I state that I didn't have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, were rifles obtained? Well, you said that you got one at the end of October.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about those other people? Did they also get weapons? Did they start to come to guard duty with weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Zoran had a hunting carbine. Ivica Kupreskic gave it to him. I also know that Mirko Sakic bought a Kalashnikov, also from those people who were coming from Jajce. Anybody could obtain weapons at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened with your guards after the conflict in November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were only a few of us there. In the beginning, we performed our guard duty regularly, you could say, but then as time went on, some of them wouldn't turn up for duty. So sometimes for two or three days, nobody went on watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there were 14 of you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at night there were six two-hour shifts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from 7.00 to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how many people were there in a shift?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Two people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that every night practically we had guard duty, so it was normal that people had their own things to do, they were tired, they would come straight for work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how did you try to resolve those problems with the guard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we agreed such problems, because in that part of our village, Zoran was -- how shall I put it -- an exemplary young man, and we all trusted him. We agreed for him to try to resolve why people were not turning up for duty, was this justified or not, could this be made up in some way. Because I can also say that when somebody was missing for two or three days -- for example, Mirjan Kupreskic goes to play somewhere, and of course he is not back for three days, so some people complained. Ivica Kupreskic too, went out on the road a lot. So because of situations like that there are problems: "He's not going to do it so I'm not going to do it," and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also make a schedule for the guard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't a schedule. We agreed, whenever anybody had time, if somebody had something to do until midnight, then we would tell him to be from 5.00 to 7.00 on duty. There was no schedule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you actually took part every day in the guards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you said that this was the way in which you tried to deal with those watches after the conflict. How long did this function, and how long did Zoran Kupreskic perform this job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, very briefly, because there were a lot of problems there. Nobody could really resolve them. So at the end of January, let's say, we agreed for me to carry on doing this work because Zoran had more obligations at Vitezit, where he was employed. So I tried to do something, but it wasn't going very well. Even later, we gave up. If something happened, if there was a Serb attack in Bugojno, in Vlasic, then we would get back to work again. But this didn't last long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if problems occurred in the surrounding area, then would you meet up again and --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But formally, at the time of the second conflict, on the 16th of April, you were in a certain way responsible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, things remained like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You are still working in Vjetrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court who Mesud Sivro is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sivro Mesud was a good friend of mine. He still is a good friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He is from Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim. We worked together in the Vjetrenice commercial company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what are your contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because we worked in the same company, he was a driver of a small truck, a small TAM truck, and very often he would drive me home from work. It was easier for me, of course. I didn't have to pay for a bus ticket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also bring some things for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, whatever I needed from Vitez. Whatever I needed to transport home, he would do that for me, and if I needed to transport something from my house somewhere, he also would help me with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What colour was that truck?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was green with a blue tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that his truck, or did it belong to the company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The truck belonged to the company, to the Vjetrenice company. He was only the driver of that truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did he come to visit you before the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Often. Very often. Well, I can tell you the days that he didn't come, but he would usually drive me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us, if you remember, before the start of the war, in February or March, whether there were any problems with Muslims in the village, that the Croat side perhaps banned the Muslims from joining the guard duty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were never banned from taking part in the guard duty. We couldn't do that. There were a few of us only, and I know that for a while we had agreed for their guards and our guards, when they were being carried out, not to go on that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not to go from the main road towards Gornji Ahmici because allegedly of the civilians who were passing. We didn't want them to be afraid. It wasn't nice to see or to meet an armed person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was an agreement which both applied to Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We agreed for us not to patrol along that road and for them not to patrol that road. There was no ban. It was an agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say that you could not prevent them from performing their guard duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were only a few of us. We really couldn't do much. There were many more of them. We wouldn't dare prevent them from anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice how many people would come out on watch duty on the Muslim side? Did they perform the guard duty in shifts of two or were there more of them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were always more of them. There were always at least four of them because there were a lot of people who were fit for military duty, who could perform such a duty, so, of course, there were more of them. Sometimes there would be five or six of them in a group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many men fit for military service there were in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the villagers who lived in Ahmici, well, I can't be precise, but about 140 to 150, approximately. Of course, I never counted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other people in the village besides the villagers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I met some people I had never seen before. Although I was from the village, there were people there I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some witnesses have said that the population of Ahmici doubled after the fall of Jajce. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it doubled, but I know that there were a lot of people who arrived whom I had never seen before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you remember the Bajram of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. Since I was in the folk-dancing company, Slobodan Princip Selo, and Zoran and Mirjan were members too, and there were Muslims with whom we were on good terms, and we went to Gornji or Upper Vitez, where we performed, and I took part in the performance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this performance? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was in Upper Vitez, called Mahala, also known as Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that? Was that a Bajram celebration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was intended to be a Bajram festival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in March, I think. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the Easter of that year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At Easter we went to Mali Mosunj, "The Way of the Cross," and we had the same kind of performance there for Easter that we had had for Bajram in the Mahala, and the Muslims went there with us, the ones who were in our company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Like every day, since I'm employed, I went to work in the morning at about 7.00, and I came back at about half past three. And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you watch Vitez television?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was unable to receive Vitez television. I still can't because this is an area where we can't catch this programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out about the kidnapping of Zivko Totic and the killing of his escort on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't hear anything?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in the evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime between 2.00 and half past 2.00, I got a telephone call from the late Nenad Santic, and he said that there were some problems and that I should come to Jozo Livancic's house. Of course I got up, I got ready, and I went to that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Jozo Livancic's house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Down below the road, the main road, that is, in the direction of Rovna. So to the left-hand side of the main road in the direction of Rovna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see Jozo Livancic's house on this aerial photograph? It should be there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it here. Just a moment. So we're going up the main road this way (indicating). It's somewhere in this area (indicating), the house of Jozo Livancic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you cross the road. It's on the other side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you encounter there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at Jozo Livancic's house, I found Jozo Livancic, and his son, Zeljo Livancic. There was Nenad Santic. Then I remember there was Anto Covic, Ivo Vujovic, and my uncle, Simo Vidovic, the late Simo Vidovic. They were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other Vidovics there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you, and anyone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was Jevco, and Ivica Vidovic, also known as Jevco.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in fact, since Jevco was in the civil defence, he said that the situation was not good, that there was some information that the Muslims might attack the Croats, and that we who were there should take our families and neighbours to a safe place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these people have any kind of duties in any kind of organisation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These people were in the civil defence. They were members of the civil defence. Each of them, each of the ones I mentioned, had the duty to, in case of trouble, to evacuate the population around their area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nenad Santic, was he a member of the civil defence, and what was his role at that meeting because you say that he invited you to the house of Jozo Livancic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he was in the civil defence, but I do know that he was a member of the HDZ and that he was well-informed about certain events that were taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who called that meeting, who called that kind of meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you can call it a meeting, it was Jevco Vidovic; Ivica Vidovic, also known as Jevco.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that Nenad Santic called the meeting? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was Jevco who communicated this to us, but whether it was Nenad who told Jevco to do that, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Very well. We shall have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, we may continue. You said that, in fact, you did not know who had called the meeting --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- whether it was Santic or Vidovic, but you were contacted by Ivica Vidovic, Jevco?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of civil defence for Ahmici, Santici, and Pirici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know it was Ivica Vidovic, also known as Jevco.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that organisation start functioning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when the Serbian planes bombed Princip and Busovaca, I think it was then that the civil defence started operating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you assigned to observe what was going on in your part of the village and organise the possible evacuation of your part of the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out in Busovaca, then Ivica Vidovic, Jevco, rang me up, in fact. In fact, he asked me whether I would agree to this, if I had enough spare time to maintain contacts with him and so on, and I accepted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all the people who were involved in the civil defence present at that meeting, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I know that Niko Sakic wasn't there, and he should have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he wasn't there? Did you ever talk to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since Niko didn't have a telephone, very likely they were unable to call him to the meeting. We were told to come to the meeting by phone, and Niko didn't have a telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Ivica Vidovic, Jevco, told you what to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He explained that there was some problems, that it was possible that we would be attacked by the Muslims, and that I should go and tell my family, my other neighbours, and that I should take them to shelters. He told me, since it was on my way, to drop in to Niko Sakic's house and tell him that he should do the same in his area, to do what I was to do in my area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I went in the direction of Niko Sakic's house. I woke him up, and I told him what I had been told by Jevco, to wake up his family, his neighbours, and take them to a shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did you go to his house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had been at Niko Sakic's house, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then I went to the Kupreskic houses. I woke up Ivica and Zoran Kupreskic, and I told them the same. I told them that they should wake up their families and all the other Kupreskics and that they should go to shelters. Then I went to my own house. I woke up my parents, my wife, and my children. I told them to get ready. I said they would have to go to the shelter. Then I went to wake up my aunt Manda, Gordana Vidovic, and her mother. When I had woken her up, I went to Slavko Vidovic's house, where Ilko Brnada was staying with his wife and two children. I woke him up and told him the same things. Since his father-in-law was in Rovna, he went to Rovna with his wife and family, and I returned to my home to fetch my parents, my wife, my children, and my aunt Manda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you take them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I got back, they were ready, so we went to Niko Sakic's shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you determine what time it was? How long was it before the gunfire broke out? What time was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was about -- well, I left my house at about ten past five, five past five. I think it was like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
